extracted.intended_audience: citizens and readers debating the proposed U.S. Constitution (readers of The Federalist, especially New York voters)
extracted.subtask_description: An argumentative essay (Federalist No. LXXXIII) evaluating how the proposed Constitution treats the judiciary and the trial by jury, defending the plan against objections and explaining practical/legal consequences. Focuses on the relation of federal and state courts, appellate jurisdiction, and whether jury trial must be constitutionally guaranteed in civil cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction of State tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts will have concurrent jurisdiction in cases arising under the laws of the Union unless expressly prohibited by future acts of the national legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author infers this from the nature of judiciary power and the general genius of the system: State courts are 'natural auxiliaries' to national law execution. The point admits exceptions for cases 'peculiar to' the Constitution or where Congress deems federal-court-only adjudication expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction extends to State tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals should lie from state courts to the Supreme Court of the United States in the enumerated classes of federal cognizance where the Supreme Court has appellate (not original) jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution gives appellate jurisdiction in enumerated cases without limiting appeals to inferior federal courts; the object of appeal—cases—rather than the originating tribunal is what matters. Excluding state-court appeals would allow evasion of national judiciary authority and subvert the plan's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional discretion over inferior tribunals' jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has authority to constitute inferior federal courts and to determine whether those courts exercise original or appellate jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Constitution provides no precise definition for subordinate courts' authority, establishment of appeals from state courts to subordinate national tribunals is within legislative discretion and may reduce the need for many separate federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence in Constitution does not equal abolition (trial by jury in civil cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution's silence regarding jury trial in civil causes should not be read as an abolition of that institution in civil cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal maxims like 'expression of one thing is the exclusion of another' have been misapplied by opponents; common-sense interpretation is required. Where a mode of trial is 'not provided for' it is not thereby abolished; the legislature still retains power to authorize juries in civil cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury in criminal cases is a primary safeguard of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision for jury trial in criminal cases is ample and is the principal judicial safeguard concerned with preserving liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitrary impeachments and prosecutorial abuses relate chiefly to criminal procedures; the Constitution's express guarantee of criminal jury trial and habeas corpus addresses the chief concerns about judicial despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature's power to constitute courts includes prescribing modes of trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A power to constitute courts implies the power to prescribe the mode of trial (e.g., whether to use juries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nothing were said in the Constitution about juries, the legislature would be free to adopt or omit them; the express command for criminal jury trial narrows that discretion only in criminal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: State practices should largely determine civil jury use under federal courts (but with difficulties)
rubrics_metrics.description: One workable rule would be that federal causes should be tried by jury if, in the State where the federal court sits, a similar case would be tried by jury in the State courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes this has practical problems because of the wide diversity of state judicial arrangements; adopting state practice as the standard risks capricious and inconsistent outcomes across the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of state judicial systems precludes a simple uniform constitutional rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Because states differ widely in the extent and form of jury trial and in the separation or blending of law, equity, and admiralty jurisdiction, it is extremely difficult to craft a single constitutional provision that would properly regulate jury trial in all federal cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay surveys state differences (e.g., New York, Pennsylvania, Connecticut, the Eastern States) to show why proposals like 'trial by jury shall be as heretofore' or narrowly phrased guarantees would be inoperative, unfair, or cause confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of particulars excludes generals (properly applied)
rubrics_metrics.description: In grants of authority, specification of particular powers excludes a general legislative authority; enumerating federal powers indicates limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The maxim is applicable where a specific grant alters a pre-existing lack of power (e.g., creating a special mode for married women's conveyance), but misapplication to jury-trial provisions (to infer abolition) is erroneous and contrary to common-sense construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury is a check against corruption but has vulnerabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury trial multiplies obstacles to corruption because persuading both bench and jury is harder than corrupting one body; nonetheless, selection processes (sheriff, clerks) create potential avenues for manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even allowing for possible corruption of juror selection officers, the double security of court and jury generally preserves institutional integrity. The practical utility of jury trial in civil matters is recognized even by the author despite reservations about essentiality to liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juries are unsuitable for matters requiring technical legal expertise or public policy (e.g., prize causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries are often incompetent and inappropriate for cases that turn wholly on the laws and usages of nations or require specialized legal/policy judgments (such as prize causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such matters may risk injuring foreign relations if juries, influenced by local impressions, fail to respect international law and policy; treaty practices often reserve final determination to high executive or specialized bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of equity from law jurisdiction is important; equity cases unsuitable for jury trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity address 'extraordinary cases' that are exceptions to general rules and require long, deliberative, intricate consideration ill-suited to jury processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merging equity into ordinary legal courts and subjecting equitable matters to jury trial would unsettle rules, encourage special determinations, and undermine both equity jurisprudence and the purity of jury trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making one State's system the national standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing one State's constitution ('trial by jury shall be as heretofore') or adopting a single State model as the standard for the Union is impracticable and likely to provoke jealousy and opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no neutral antecedent 'heretofore' for the United States as a whole because the federal government has no prior judiciary; choosing any State as a model risks partiality and political difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: A universal constitutional guarantee of jury trial in all cases would be inadvisable
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserting a constitutional provision establishing jury trial in all cases would be a grave error, given precedents and the varied needs of different causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No member of the Union provides for jury trial in all cases; such a blanket rule would be unworkable and could encumber the national government with impracticable obligations.
